quirks_found: Nondeterministic dedup: ROW_NUMBER() ordered only by _loaded_at DESC has no tie-breaker, so when rows for the same order_id share the same latest _loaded_at, which row survives is arbitrary.

NULL _loaded_at handling depends on the engine. In Snowflake or Postgres, DESC puts NULLs first, so a row with a NULL _loaded_at would 'win' over properly timestamped loads. The model makes this explicit with NULLS FIRST.
Rows with NULL order_id all fall into a single partition, so only one NULL-order_id row is kept and the rest are silently dropped.
TRIM only removes spaces, so tabs, newlines and non-breaking spaces stay in status. Values that differ only by such characters are not fully normalised.
LOWER(TRIM(status)) leaves NULL status as NULL and turns an all-space status into an empty string '' rather than NULL.
_loaded_at is used only for dedup and is not output, so downstream consumers cannot see which load version was kept.
jobs.model_sql:
with tmp_ranked as (
    select
        o.*,
        row_number() over (
            partition by order_id
            order by _loaded_at desc nulls first
        ) as rn
    from {{ source('raw', 'orders') }} o
)
select
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    order_ts,
    lower(trim(status)) as status,
    channel,
    promo_code
from tmp_ranked
where rn = 1

quirks_found: first_order_date is the minimum over all raw orders regardless of status. Cancelled, failed or test orders still count toward a customer's first order date.
raw.orders is used as-is (not deduplicated or cleaned). Duplicate loads don't change the MIN, but bad or late-loaded rows with an early order_ts would.
The timestamp is cast to DATE after taking the MIN. The date reflects whatever timezone or offset order_ts is stored in; no timezone conversion is applied.
Customers with no orders, or whose orders all have NULL order_ts, get NULL first_order_date because of the LEFT JOIN.
Orders whose customer_id has no match in raw.customers are silently dropped.
raw.customers is not deduplicated. Duplicate customer_id rows in the source appear as duplicate rows in the output, each with the same first_order_date.
Customer rows with a NULL customer_id are kept, with NULL first_order_date, because the LEFT JOIN on NULL never matches.
jobs.model_sql:
with tmp_first as (
    select
        customer_id,
        min(order_ts)::date as first_order_date
    from {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}
    where customer_id is not null
    group by customer_id
)

select
    c.customer_id,
    c.region,
    c.segment,
    c.signup_date,
    c.marketing_opt_in,
    f.first_order_date
from {{ source('raw', 'customers') }} c
left join tmp_first f
    on f.customer_id = c.customer_id

quirks_found: The header says 'captured payments', but there is no capture or status filter; raw.payments has no status column. Every payment row with amount > 0 is counted, whatever its outcome.
The filter amount > 0 silently drops refunds and negative adjustments, so gross_revenue is not net of refunds. Rows with a NULL amount are also dropped, because NULL > 0 is not true.
Rows with a NULL paid_ts are not filtered out. They are grouped into a single revenue_date = NULL row.
No deduplication on payment_id. Duplicate payment rows, such as re-loaded records, are double-counted in both gross_revenue and payments.
The paid_ts::DATE cast truncates to a calendar day in whatever time zone the timestamp or session uses. There is no explicit business-time-zone conversion.
Days with no qualifying payments get no row at all, rather than a row with 0 revenue.
jobs.model_sql:
SELECT paid_ts::DATE AS revenue_date, SUM(amount) AS gross_revenue, COUNT(*) AS payments
FROM {{ source('raw', 'payments') }}
WHERE amount > 0
GROUP BY 1

quirks_found: A NULL list_price fails both comparisons and falls through to ELSE, so it is labelled 'premium'.
Band boundaries are exclusive on the upper end: a price of exactly 50 is 'mid' and exactly 200 is 'premium'.
WHERE is_active silently drops rows where is_active is NULL, not just rows where it is false.
No deduplication on product_id. Duplicate product rows in raw.products pass straight through to the dimension.
Negative list_price values are labelled 'budget' with no validation.
jobs.model_sql:
SELECT product_id, category, list_price,
       CASE WHEN list_price < 50 THEN 'budget'
            WHEN list_price < 200 THEN 'mid'
            ELSE 'premium' END AS price_band
FROM {{ source('raw', 'products') }}
WHERE is_active

quirks_found: Customers with NULL marketing_opt_in are excluded, because the WHERE clause on a NULL boolean filters them out.
Rows in raw.customers with a NULL customer_id survive the DELETE (NULL IN (...) is never true), so they stay in the audience.
Duplicate customer_id rows in raw.customers are not deduplicated and appear more than once in the audience.
The return reason match is exact and case-sensitive ('damaged'). Variants such as 'Damaged' or ' damaged ' do not exclude a customer.
Exclusion uses raw.orders rather than stg_orders_clean, so orders of any status (cancelled, test, duplicate loads) with a damaged return still exclude the customer.
Returns whose order_id does not exist in raw.orders are silently ignored by the inner join.
Any damaged return at any time excludes the customer permanently. There is no time window.
jobs.model_sql:
WITH audience AS (
  SELECT customer_id, region, segment
  FROM {{ source('raw', 'customers') }}
  WHERE marketing_opt_in
),
damaged_customers AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id
  FROM {{ source('raw', 'returns') }} r
  JOIN {{ source('raw', 'orders') }} o ON o.order_id = r.order_id
  WHERE r.reason = 'damaged' AND o.customer_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT a.customer_id, a.region, a.segment
FROM audience a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM damaged_customers d WHERE d.customer_id = a.customer_id
)

quirks_found: NULL promo codes are relabelled 'none'. They merge with any real promo code whose value is the literal 'none'.
Empty-string or whitespace promo codes are not normalised. They appear as their own group, separate from 'none'.
Promo codes are grouped case-sensitively and without trimming, so 'SAVE10' and 'save10 ' count as different codes.
There is no status filter, so cancelled, refunded or failed orders count toward orders and buyers.
raw.orders appears to be a load table (_loaded_at), so it may hold duplicate rows per order. COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) hides these duplicates.
If the same order_id appears under different promo codes across reloads, it is counted in each of those groups.
COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) ignores NULL customer_id. Orders without a customer add to orders but not to buyers.
COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) ignores NULL order_id rows.
jobs.model_sql:
SELECT COALESCE(promo_code, 'none') AS promo_code,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS buyers
FROM {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}
GROUP BY 1

quirks_found: The sign is flipped with -SUM(amount), which assumes refund amounts are stored as negatives. Any refund stored as a positive amount produces a negative 'refunded' value, and mixed-sign rows partially cancel each other out.
Payments with a NULL paid_ts are grouped into a single row with refund_date = NULL.
COUNT(*) counts every refund row, including rows where amount is NULL, so 'refunds' can exceed the number of rows that contribute to 'refunded'.
If every amount for a date is NULL, 'refunded' is NULL instead of 0.
The filter method = 'refund' is a case-sensitive exact match. Variants such as 'Refund', 'REFUND' or values with trailing spaces are excluded, and rows with a NULL method are excluded.
No deduplication on payment_id, so duplicate payment rows are double-counted in both 'refunded' and 'refunds'.
Dates with no refunds have no row at all; they are not zero-filled.
Refunds are attributed to the payment date (paid_ts), not to the original order date or the date in the returns table.
jobs.model_sql:
SELECT paid_ts::DATE AS refund_date, -SUM(amount) AS refunded, COUNT(*) AS refunds
FROM {{ source('raw', 'payments') }}
WHERE method = 'refund'
GROUP BY 1

quirks_found: Returns are only counted when the order's _loaded_at exactly equals its order_ts (o._loaded_at = o.order_ts in the join). This is likely a bug and probably excludes most returns.
There is no lower bound on the 60-day window. Returns with return_ts before order_ts are still counted. Returns with a NULL return_ts are excluded.
Duplicate rows in raw.orders that share an order_id (and pass the _loaded_at = order_ts check) fan out the returns join and inflate units_returned.
Duplicate product_id rows in raw.products fan out both the sold and the returned sums.
Returns are not tied to specific order_items lines. A returned product does not have to appear in the order's items.
Products with a NULL category are grouped together as a NULL-category row in tmp_sold. USING (category) never matches NULL, so that row always shows units_returned = 0.
Categories that have returns but no sales are dropped, because the LEFT JOIN starts from tmp_sold.
If units_sold is 0 or NULL, return_rate is NULL; DuckDB returns NULL on division by zero rather than raising an error.
return_rate is ROUND(... * 1.0 / units_sold, 4), a decimal rounded to 4 places. The rounding and the resulting type are kept as is.
Order status is ignored. Cancelled orders still count toward units sold and returns.
jobs.model_sql:
WITH tmp_sold AS (
    SELECT p.category, SUM(i.quantity) AS units_sold
    FROM {{ source('raw', 'order_items') }} i
    JOIN {{ source('raw', 'products') }} p USING (product_id)
    GROUP BY 1
),
tmp_ret AS (
    SELECT p.category, SUM(r.quantity) AS units_returned
    FROM {{ source('raw', 'returns') }} r
    JOIN {{ source('raw', 'orders') }} o ON o.order_id = r.order_id AND o._loaded_at = o.order_ts
    JOIN {{ source('raw', 'products') }} p ON p.product_id = r.product_id
    WHERE r.return_ts <= o.order_ts + INTERVAL 60 DAY
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT s.category, s.units_sold, COALESCE(r.units_returned, 0) AS units_returned,
       ROUND(COALESCE(r.units_returned, 0) * 1.0 / s.units_sold, 4) AS return_rate
FROM tmp_sold s LEFT JOIN tmp_ret r USING (category)

quirks_found: Rows with NULL reason are not filtered out. They form their own group per month with reason = NULL.
Rows with NULL return_ts are not filtered out. They are aggregated into a row with month = NULL.
No deduplication on return_id, so duplicate return rows in raw.returns are counted twice in units.
SUM(quantity) returns NULL for a group where every quantity is NULL, rather than 0. Negative or zero quantities are summed as-is.
The output column is named 'month', which is a SQL keyword or function name and may need quoting in downstream queries on some engines.

sessions uses COUNT(*), which counts raw rows rather than distinct session_id. Duplicate session rows in raw.web_sessions (for example from reloads) inflate the session count, and their pageviews are summed again.
Rows with a NULL source are kept and grouped into their own NULL-source bucket rather than labelled (for example as 'unknown') or dropped.
Rows with a NULL started_at fall into a NULL month bucket instead of being excluded.
SUM(pageviews) ignores NULL pageviews but still counts those sessions. A group where every pageviews value is NULL gets pageviews = NULL, not 0.
No filtering is applied (for example on customer_id IS NULL or on bot traffic), so all sessions, including anonymous ones, are counted.
jobs.model_sql:
with tmp_sessions as (
    select
        cast(date_trunc('month', started_at) as date) as month,
        source,
        pageviews
    from {{ source('raw', 'web_sessions') }}
)

select
    month,
    source,
    count(*) as sessions,
    sum(pageviews) as pageviews
from tmp_sessions
group by month, source

quirks_found: WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' also drops orders whose status is NULL, because a NULL comparison is not true.
Inner join to raw.products silently drops order items whose product_id is missing from products, and their revenue is excluded from both the category and the month totals.
If raw.products has duplicate product_id rows, the join fans out and multiplies revenue for those items.
Products with a NULL category are grouped together into a single NULL-category row.
share_of_month is rounded to 4 decimals, so shares within a month may not sum exactly to 1.
If a month's total revenue is 0, the share division produces NULL (DuckDB) or an error, depending on the engine.
Uses raw.order_items quantity*unit_price (list-line revenue) without netting out returns or discounts.
jobs.model_sql:
with tmp_cat as (
    select
        date_trunc('month', o.order_ts)::date as month,
        p.category,
        sum(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as revenue
    from {{ source('raw', 'order_items') }} i
    join {{ ref('stg_orders_clean') }} o on o.order_id = i.order_id
    join {{ source('raw', 'products') }} p on p.product_id = i.product_id
    where o.status <> 'cancelled'
    group by 1, 2
)
select
    month,
    category,
    revenue,
    round(revenue / sum(revenue) over (partition by month), 4) as share_of_month
from tmp_cat

quirks_found: The filter status <> 'cancelled' also drops rows where status is NULL, because a NULL comparison is not true. Only an exact lowercase 'cancelled' is excluded, so values like 'Cancelled' or 'CANCELLED' are counted as valid orders.

Orders with a NULL order_ts get a NULL quarter. They are aggregated in tmp_q but then silently dropped by JOIN ... USING (quarter), because NULL never equals NULL. They do not appear in the output at all.
Orders with a NULL channel are kept as their own NULL-channel group and count toward the quarter total.
share is rounded to 4 decimal places per row, so the shares within a quarter may not sum to exactly 1.
Quarter totals are recomputed from the filtered, grouped counts. Shares are therefore relative to non-cancelled orders with a known status only, not to all orders.
jobs.model_sql:
with tmp_q as (
    select
        date_trunc('quarter', order_ts)::date as quarter,
        channel,
        count(*) as orders
    from {{ ref('stg_orders_clean') }}
    where status <> 'cancelled'
    group by 1, 2
),

tmp_q_tot as (
    select
        quarter,
        sum(orders) as total_orders
    from tmp_q
    group by quarter
)

select
    q.quarter,
    q.channel,
    q.orders,
    round(q.orders * 1.0 / t.total_orders, 4) as share
from tmp_q q
join tmp_q_tot t using (quarter)

quirks_found: The INNER JOIN to tmp_items drops every order that has no order_items rows, so those orders are missing from order_totals entirely.
gross_amount and units are not COALESCEd. If every line for an order has a NULL quantity or unit_price, the value is NULL, and individual NULL lines are silently skipped in the SUM.
If a payment amount is NULL, the CASE sends it to the ELSE 0 branch, so it adds nothing to captured or refunded. Zero-amount payments are likewise ignored.
net_revenue is captured minus refunded from payments only. It does not use gross_amount, so it can differ from the item totals.
Payments are summed with no deduplication. Duplicate payment rows, for example a reloaded payment_id, would inflate captured and refunded.
Duplicate order_ids in stg_orders_clean, if any, would produce duplicate output rows. There is no dedup on the order side.
Payments with a NULL order_id, or for orders not in stg_orders_clean, are dropped silently.
jobs.model_sql:
WITH tmp_items AS (
    SELECT order_id,
           SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_amount,
           SUM(quantity) AS units
    FROM {{ source('raw', 'order_items') }}
    GROUP BY order_id
),
tmp_pay AS (
    SELECT order_id,
           SUM(CASE WHEN amount > 0 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS captured,
           SUM(CASE WHEN amount < 0 THEN -amount ELSE 0 END) AS refunded
    FROM {{ source('raw', 'payments') }}
    GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.customer_id,
       o.order_ts,
       o.status,
       o.channel,
       i.gross_amount,
       i.units,
       COALESCE(p.captured, 0) AS captured,
       COALESCE(p.refunded, 0) AS refunded,
       COALESCE(p.captured, 0) - COALESCE(p.refunded, 0) AS net_revenue
FROM {{ ref('stg_orders_clean') }} o
JOIN tmp_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN tmp_pay p ON p.order_id = o.order_id

quirks_found: repeat_pct uses integer division (//), so the percentage is truncated rather than rounded. The script marks this as intentional.
status <> 'cancelled' also drops orders whose status is NULL, because a NULL comparison is not true.

The 'new buyer' cohort is based on a customer's first non-cancelled order, not their first order overall. A customer whose real first order was cancelled is placed in the month of their first non-cancelled order.
Customers with a NULL customer_id are excluded entirely.
A second order with the exact same timestamp as the first (including duplicate order rows) counts as a repeat within 30 days, since next_ts <= order_ts + 30 days holds.
The 30-day window is inclusive (<=) and compares full timestamps, not calendar days.
Customers with no later order (next_ts NULL) count as non-repeat through the ELSE 0 branch.
Ties on order_ts are broken by order_id. Rows with a NULL order_id sort last under DuckDB's default NULLS LAST.

The most recent cohort months have not yet had a full 30 days to observe repeats, so their repeat_pct is biased low. The results also depend on when the job runs, although the SQL itself does not reference the current time.
If order_ts is TIMESTAMPTZ, DATE_TRUNC('month') and the ::DATE cast depend on the session time zone.
jobs.model_sql:
WITH tmp_seq AS (
    SELECT customer_id, order_ts,
           LEAD(order_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts, order_id) AS next_ts,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts, order_id) AS n
    FROM {{ ref('stg_orders_clean') }}
    WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL AND status <> 'cancelled'
)
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_ts)::DATE AS cohort_month,
       COUNT(*) AS new_buyers,
       SUM(CASE WHEN next_ts <= order_ts + INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS repeat_30d,
       (SUM(CASE WHEN next_ts <= order_ts + INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100) // COUNT(*) AS repeat_pct
FROM tmp_seq
WHERE n = 1
GROUP BY 1

quirks_found: status <> 'cancelled' also drops orders whose status is NULL, because the comparison evaluates to NULL.
The attribution window is asymmetric: a session starting exactly at order_ts counts, but one starting exactly 7 days before does not.
The latest session is picked first and then COALESCE is applied. If that session's source is NULL, the order shows 'unattributed' even when an earlier session in the window has a non-NULL source.
Sessions with NULL started_at or NULL customer_id never match any order.
Ties on started_at are broken by the highest session_id. If session_id is also NULL, the pick depends on how NULLs are ordered.
Sessions after the order timestamp are ignored, and there is no fallback to sessions older than 7 days.
Duplicate rows in stg_orders_clean are not deduplicated, so each one gets its own attribution row.
jobs.model_sql:
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_ts,
       COALESCE((
         SELECT s.source
         FROM {{ source('raw', 'web_sessions') }} s
         WHERE s.customer_id = o.customer_id
           AND s.started_at <= o.order_ts
           AND s.started_at > o.order_ts - INTERVAL 7 DAY
         ORDER BY s.started_at DESC, s.session_id DESC
         LIMIT 1
       ), 'unattributed') AS last_touch_source
FROM {{ ref('stg_orders_clean') }} o
WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL AND o.status <> 'cancelled'

quirks_found: Inner joins drop order items whose order is missing from stg_orders_clean and orders whose customer is missing from raw.customers.
Duplicate customer_id rows in raw.customers would fan out and multiply units. Duplicate order_ids in stg_orders_clean would do the same.
Customers with a NULL region are grouped together into a single NULL region, which can appear in the top-5 output.
Order items with a NULL product_id form their own group and can be ranked.
SUM(quantity) is NULL if all quantities in a group are NULL. Where such rows land under ORDER BY units DESC depends on the engine's default NULL ordering.
Returns are not subtracted: units counts gross quantity ordered, filtered only by whatever stg_orders_clean keeps.
ROW_NUMBER is used rather than RANK, so ties on units are broken by the lowest product_id and exactly 5 rows are kept per region.
jobs.model_sql:
with tmp_units as (
  select c.region, i.product_id, sum(i.quantity) as units
  from {{ source('raw', 'order_items') }} i
  join {{ ref('stg_orders_clean') }} o on o.order_id = i.order_id
  join {{ source('raw', 'customers') }} c on c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  group by 1, 2
)
select region, product_id, units, rnk from (
  select *, row_number() over (partition by region order by units desc, product_id) as rnk
  from tmp_units
) ranked
where rnk <= 5

quirks_found: NOT IN subquery: if daily_revenue contains any row with a NULL revenue_date, the NOT IN evaluates to NULL for every row, so the INSERT adds no refund-only days at all.
Refund rows with a NULL refund_date are never inserted, because NULL NOT IN (...) is never true. Those refunds are silently dropped from the reconciliation.

If refunds_daily has more than one row for the same refund_date, the LEFT JOIN fans out and repeats that day's gross_revenue. Refund-only days would also be inserted more than once. Totals would then be inflated.
Days in daily_revenue with a NULL revenue_date are kept, with refunded = 0, because the join on NULL never matches.
If gross_revenue is NULL, net_revenue is NULL, since only refunded is COALESCEd.
Refund-only days get gross_revenue = 0 rather than NULL.
If refunded is NULL on a refund-only row, refunded and net_revenue stay NULL there (no COALESCE in the INSERT). On joined rows, a NULL refunded is coalesced to 0.
The target table has no ORDER BY, so row order is undefined. Refund-only days are appended after the revenue days rather than interleaved by date.
jobs.model_sql:
with base as (
    select d.revenue_date as day,
           d.gross_revenue,
           coalesce(r.refunded, 0) as refunded,
           d.gross_revenue - coalesce(r.refunded, 0) as net_revenue
    from {{ ref('daily_revenue') }} d
    left join {{ ref('refunds_daily') }} r on r.refund_date = d.revenue_date
),
refund_only as (
    select r.refund_date as day,
           0 as gross_revenue,
           r.refunded as refunded,
           -r.refunded as net_revenue
    from {{ ref('refunds_daily') }} r
    where r.refund_date not in (select revenue_date from {{ ref('daily_revenue') }})
)
select day, gross_revenue, refunded, net_revenue from base
union all
select day, gross_revenue, refunded, net_revenue from refund_only

quirks_found: WHERE t.status <> 'cancelled' also drops orders with NULL status, because NULL <> 'cancelled' evaluates to NULL.
The status comparison is case-sensitive. Variants such as 'Cancelled' or 'CANCELLED' are not excluded.
The inner join to raw.customers drops orders whose customer_id is missing from customers or is NULL.
If raw.customers has duplicate customer_id rows (it is the raw table, not deduplicated), matching orders are counted more than once. This inflates orders and weights the AOV.
COUNT(*) counts orders with NULL gross_amount, but AVG ignores them. The orders column and the AOV denominator can therefore differ.
Customers with NULL segment or region are grouped into NULL segment/region rows rather than being excluded.
jobs.model_sql:
SELECT c.segment, c.region, COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(AVG(t.gross_amount), 2) AS aov
FROM {{ ref('order_totals') }} t
JOIN {{ source('raw', 'customers') }} c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
WHERE t.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY 1, 2

quirks_found: The filter status <> 'cancelled' also drops orders whose status is NULL, because a NULL comparison is never true. Those orders are left out of lifetime counts and revenue.
The status match is case-sensitive. Values such as 'Cancelled' or 'CANCELLED' are not excluded and are counted as live orders.
COUNT(*) counts every non-cancelled order, including orders with NULL net_revenue. A customer can therefore have lifetime_orders > 0 while lifetime_net_revenue is 0.
COALESCE(SUM(net_revenue), 0) turns a sum that is NULL (all of the customer's net_revenue values are NULL) into 0. This makes such customers look the same as customers with genuinely zero revenue.
Customers with no qualifying orders get lifetime_orders = 0 and lifetime_net_revenue = 0, but first_order and last_order stay NULL (these two columns are not coalesced).
Orders whose customer_id is not in dim_customers are silently dropped by the LEFT JOIN from dim_customers.
If dim_customers ever contains duplicate customer_id rows, the output repeats those customers and their aggregates.
first_order and last_order are truncated to DATE, so time-of-day and any timezone context are lost. If order_ts is a timestamptz, the date depends on the session timezone.
jobs.model_sql:
with tmp_agg as (
    select
        customer_id,
        count(*) as lifetime_orders,
        sum(net_revenue) as lifetime_net_revenue,
        min(order_ts)::date as first_order,
        max(order_ts)::date as last_order
    from {{ ref('order_totals') }}
    where status <> 'cancelled' and customer_id is not null
    group by customer_id
)
select
    d.customer_id,
    d.region,
    d.segment,
    coalesce(a.lifetime_orders, 0) as lifetime_orders,
    coalesce(a.lifetime_net_revenue, 0) as lifetime_net_revenue,
    a.first_order,
    a.last_order
from {{ ref('dim_customers') }} d
left join tmp_agg a on a.customer_id = d.customer_id

quirks_found: The week spine comes only from web_sessions. Weeks that have orders but no sessions are silently dropped, along with their orders and revenue.
The filter status <> 'cancelled' also drops orders whose status is NULL.
Orders with a NULL order_ts fall into a NULL week. That week never matches the spine through the USING join, so those orders are lost.

If any web_session has a NULL started_at, the output gets a row with week NULL, orders 0, net_revenue 0 and sessions NULL. The NULL key never matches in the join, even though tmp_sessions_w has a NULL-week group with a count.
sessions is never back-filled with 0, unlike orders and net_revenue. This is only visible on the NULL-week row.
net_revenue is set to 0 both for weeks with no orders and for weeks where every order's net_revenue is NULL, so the two cases cannot be told apart.
Week boundaries depend on the engine's DATE_TRUNC('week') convention. DuckDB uses ISO weeks starting on Monday.
jobs.model_sql:
with tmp_weeks as (
    select distinct date_trunc('week', started_at)::date as week
    from {{ source('raw', 'web_sessions') }}
),
tmp_orders_w as (
    select date_trunc('week', order_ts)::date as week, count(*) as orders, sum(net_revenue) as net_revenue
    from {{ ref('order_totals') }}
    where status <> 'cancelled'
    group by 1
),
tmp_sessions_w as (
    select date_trunc('week', started_at)::date as week, count(*) as sessions
    from {{ source('raw', 'web_sessions') }}
    group by 1
)
select
    w.week,
    case when o.orders is null then 0 else o.orders end as orders,
    case when o.net_revenue is null then 0 else o.net_revenue end as net_revenue,
    s.sessions
from tmp_weeks w
left join tmp_orders_w o using (week)
left join tmp_sessions_w s using (week)

quirks_found: The lapsed cutoff is hardcoded to DATE '2026-05-01' rather than relative to the run date, so statuses go stale over time.
'lapsed' overrides 'prospect' because UPDATE 2 runs after UPDATE 1. A row with lifetime_orders = 0 and an old non-NULL last_order ends up 'lapsed'.
VIP only applies to rows still 'active'. High-revenue lapsed customers stay 'lapsed', and zero-order rows are never VIP.
Rows with NULL last_order and NULL or non-zero lifetime_orders are never lapsed. They stay 'active', or become 'vip' if revenue >= 2500.
NULL lifetime_net_revenue never qualifies as VIP.
If last_order is a timestamp, comparing it to a DATE literal relies on implicit casting. Any time on 2026-05-01 itself counts as not lapsed.
jobs.model_sql:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    lifetime_orders,
    lifetime_net_revenue,
    last_order,
    CASE
        WHEN last_order < DATE '2026-05-01' THEN 'lapsed'
        WHEN lifetime_orders = 0 THEN 'prospect'
        WHEN lifetime_net_revenue >= 2500 THEN 'vip'
        ELSE 'active'
    END AS status
FROM {{ ref('customer_orders_summary') }}

quirks_found: Customers with a NULL segment are always banded 'low'. The UPDATE join t.segment = b.segment never matches NULL, even though QUANTILE_CONT does build a threshold row for the NULL segment group.
Customers with NULL lifetime_net_revenue are always 'low' because the comparison against the thresholds is NULL. QUANTILE_CONT also ignores those NULLs when it computes the thresholds.
If every revenue in a segment is NULL, p50 and p90 are NULL and the whole segment stays 'low'.
QUANTILE_CONT interpolates, so thresholds may be values that no customer actually has. The comparisons use >=, so ties at the threshold move up a band.
For a segment with a single customer (or identical revenues), p50 = p90 = that value, so every customer in the segment is banded 'high'.
Customers with negative lifetime net revenue (heavy refunds) can still land in 'mid' or 'high' if their whole segment is negative, because the thresholds are relative to each segment.
Thresholds are computed only over customers with lifetime_orders > 0, the same filter as the banded population. Customers with zero orders are excluded from the output entirely.
jobs.model_sql:
with thresholds as (
    select segment,
           quantile_cont(lifetime_net_revenue, 0.5) as p50,
           quantile_cont(lifetime_net_revenue, 0.9) as p90
    from {{ ref('customer_orders_summary') }}
    where lifetime_orders > 0
    group by segment
),
base as (
    select customer_id, segment, lifetime_net_revenue, 'low' as band
    from {{ ref('customer_orders_summary') }}
    where lifetime_orders > 0
)
select b.customer_id,
       b.segment,
       b.lifetime_net_revenue,
       case
           when b.lifetime_net_revenue >= t.p90 then 'high'
           when b.lifetime_net_revenue >= t.p50 then 'mid'
           else b.band
       end as band
from base b
left join thresholds t
  on t.segment = b.segment
